The list kept all of them reachable, so the garbage collector could not free them and the run ended with OutOfMemoryError. Writing screenshots to disk and keeping only the file paths fixed it.

questions.question: What happens internally when System.out.println() is executed?
questions.answer: Read the statement in three parts. System is a final class in the java.lang package, which is imported automatically. out is a public static final field of the System class; its type is PrintStream, and it is connected to the standard output, normally the console. Because it is static, it is used through the class name without creating an object. println() is an instance method of the PrintStream class. It is overloaded for every kind of argument: String, int, char, double, boolean, Object and others, and the compiler chooses the version that matches. Internally: the argument is converted to text, using String.valueOf(), which calls toString() for objects and gives "null" for a null reference; the text is written to the underlying output stream; then a line separator is added, which is the difference from print(). The method is synchronized, so lines from different threads are not mixed within one call, and the stream is flushed. Related: System.err is the standard error stream and System.in is the standard input stream. Because console output is relatively slow and synchronized, frameworks use a logging library instead of println for real logging.

questions.question: Write a program that accepts input at runtime and displays the output.
questions.answer: The usual way to read input while a program runs is the Scanner class from java.util. Create it on the standard input stream, new Scanner(System.in), and call the method for the type of value expected: nextLine() for a whole line of text, next() for one word, nextInt(), nextDouble() and nextBoolean() for those types. A well-known trap: nextInt() reads the number but leaves the Enter key in the input, so a following nextLine() returns an empty string; call nextLine() once more to consume it, or read every value with nextLine() and convert it with Integer.parseInt(). hasNextLine() and hasNextInt() check whether input is available and of the right type before reading. Close the Scanner when finished. Other ways to accept input: command-line arguments, which arrive in the String[] args of main; BufferedReader with InputStreamReader, which is faster for large input; and system properties passed with -D, which is how test frameworks usually receive values such as the browser name.

questions.question: How many String objects are created by String s1 = new String("JAVA");?
questions.answer: Two objects at most, and one reference variable. The literal "JAVA" is a String object in the String Constant Pool. It is created when the class is loaded, if the pool does not already contain that text. The new keyword then always creates a second, separate String object in the normal heap, with the same characters, and s1 refers to that heap object. So the complete answer is: two objects if "JAVA" was not yet in the pool, and one object (only the heap one) if the literal was already there, for example from an earlier line. s1 itself is not an object; it is a reference. By comparison, String s2 = "JAVA"; creates no new object if the literal exists, and simply points to the pooled one. That is why s1 == s2 is false, since they are different objects, while s1.equals(s2) is true. Calling s1.intern() returns the pooled object, so s1.intern() == s2 is true. Using new String("...") is unnecessary in normal code, because it only creates an extra object.

questions.question: How do you implement hashCode() and equals()?
questions.answer: By default, equals() from the Object class compares references, so two separate objects with the same data are not equal. Override it when objects should be compared by their content. Implementing equals(Object o): (1) return true if o is the same object (this == o); (2) return false if o is null or of a different class; (3) cast o and compare each field that defines equality, using == for primitives and Objects.equals() for object fields, which is null-safe. Implementing hashCode(): return a number calculated from the same fields used in equals(), most simply with Objects.hash(field1, field2). The contract that links them: if two objects are equal according to equals(), they must return the same hashCode(). The reverse is not required; unequal objects may share a hash code, which is a collision. Always override both together. If only equals() is overridden, two equal objects have different hash codes, and HashMap and HashSet look for them in different buckets: a HashSet then keeps duplicates and map.get() fails to find an equal key. Use fields that do not change for objects used as keys. IDEs can generate both methods, Lombok offers @EqualsAndHashCode, and a Java record provides them automatically.

questions.question: How have you implemented abstraction and encapsulation in your project?
questions.answer: Encapsulation in a framework: fields are private and are reached only through public methods. In page classes the locators (By fields or @FindBy elements) are private, and the class exposes public action methods such as login() or getErrorMessage(); tests cannot touch the locators, so a locator change stays inside one class. POJO classes used for API request and response data have private fields with getters and setters. The WebDriver is kept private inside a DriverManager, in a ThreadLocal, and is reached only through getDriver(). Configuration values are private in a ConfigReader with a get(key) method. Abstraction in a framework: callers see what something does, not how. Tests call loginPage.login(user, password) without knowing which elements are located or which waits are used. The WebDriver interface is itself an abstraction: the same test code runs on Chrome, Firefox or a remote Grid. An abstract BasePage declares common behaviour, with abstract methods such as isLoaded() that each page must implement. Interfaces define contracts such as a DataReader implemented separately for Excel, JSON and CSV. Wrapper methods such as click(locator) hide the wait, the scroll and the retry. In short: encapsulation hides and protects the data; abstraction hides the implementation.
questions.realTimeExample: When the login button's id changed, only the private locator in LoginPage was edited (encapsulation). When test data moved from Excel to JSON, tests kept calling reader.read() and only the implementation behind the DataReader interface was swapped (abstraction).

type user2 into #username, click #login

Other source: [userA, userB]

questions.question: What is polymorphism? Explain compile-time versus run-time polymorphism (static versus dynamic binding) with implementation.
questions.answer: Polymorphism means one name with many forms: the same method call behaves differently depending on its arguments or on the object it is called on. Binding is the step that connects a method call to the actual method body. Compile-time polymorphism (static or early binding): the compiler decides which method will run, from the method name and the types of the arguments. It is achieved by method overloading. Static, private and final methods are also bound at compile time, because they cannot be overridden. It is slightly faster, since nothing needs to be decided while the program runs. Run-time polymorphism (dynamic or late binding): the JVM decides which method will run, at the moment of the call, from the actual type of the object, not the type of the reference variable. It is achieved by method overriding, and needs inheritance or an interface with a parent-type reference holding a child object. It is what allows one piece of code to work with many implementations. One more distinction: only instance methods are bound dynamically; fields and static methods are always resolved from the reference type.
questions.realTimeExample: driver.findElement(By.id("x")) and driver.findElement(By.xpath("//x")) use the same method with different By objects. And 'WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver()' followed by driver.get(url) runs ChromeDriver's code, chosen at run time; changing to new FirefoxDriver() changes the behaviour without changing the call.

questions.question: Where have you used inheritance in your framework?
questions.answer: Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend the code of another class with the extends keyword, so common code is written once. Typical uses in an automation framework: (1) BaseTest: holds @BeforeMethod and @AfterMethod for starting and quitting the browser, reading configuration and reporting. Every test class extends BaseTest and gets this for free. (2) BasePage: holds the driver, the wait and common wrapper methods such as click(), type(), getText() and waitForVisible(). Every page class extends BasePage. (3) Selenium itself: ChromeDriver and EdgeDriver extend ChromiumDriver, which extends RemoteWebDriver. (4) Custom exceptions extend Exception or RuntimeException. (5) Listener and utility classes may extend a base class. Java supports single, multilevel and hierarchical inheritance for classes; a class cannot extend two classes, although it can implement many interfaces. Guideline: use inheritance only for a true 'is-a' relationship, such as 'LoginPage is a page'. For 'has-a' relationships, prefer composition, where a class holds an object of another class as a field, for example a page that has a HeaderComponent. Deep inheritance chains make frameworks hard to follow.
questions.realTimeExample: Forty test classes extend BaseTest. When the team added a screenshot-on-failure step, it was written once in BaseTest's @AfterMethod and all forty classes received it without being edited.

questions.question: What are abstract classes and abstract methods? Can an abstract class contain implemented methods, and why is it allowed to have a constructor?
questions.answer: An abstract method is declared with the abstract keyword and has no body, only a signature ending in a semicolon. It states what subclasses must do without saying how. An abstract class is a class declared with the abstract keyword. It cannot be instantiated with new; it exists to be extended. Yes, it can contain implemented (concrete) methods as well as abstract ones, and it may even have no abstract methods at all. It can also have fields, static members and constructors. A class that has at least one abstract method must be declared abstract. The first concrete subclass must implement all inherited abstract methods, otherwise it too must be abstract. An abstract method cannot be private, static or final, because it has to be overridden. Why a constructor is allowed: although you cannot create an object of the abstract class directly, it is still part of every subclass object. When a subclass object is created, the subclass constructor calls the abstract class's constructor through super(), and that constructor initializes the fields the abstract class owns. So the constructor is not for creating the abstract class on its own, but for setting up its share of the child objects.
questions.realTimeExample: BasePage is abstract: it has a constructor that stores the driver and creates the wait, concrete click() and type() methods, and an abstract isLoaded() method. LoginPage and HomePage must each implement isLoaded(), and nobody can write new BasePage(driver).

questions.question: What is an interface, what is its purpose, and how have you implemented interfaces in your framework?
questions.answer: An interface is a contract: a list of methods that a class promises to provide. A class takes on the contract with the implements keyword and must supply a body for every abstract method. Method declarations in an interface are public and abstract by default, and its variables are public static final constants. Since Java 8 an interface can also contain default methods and static methods with bodies, and since Java 9 private methods. Purpose: (1) abstraction, since callers depend on what can be done and not on a specific class; (2) multiple inheritance of type, since a class can implement many interfaces although it can extend only one class; (3) loose coupling, since one implementation can be replaced with another without changing the calling code; (4) a common standard that unrelated classes can follow. In Selenium: WebDriver, WebElement, JavascriptExecutor, TakesScreenshot, Alert and SearchContext are all interfaces. In TestNG: ITestListener, IRetryAnalyzer and IAnnotationTransformer are interfaces that your classes implement. In a framework you write your own, for example a DataReader interface with Excel and JSON implementations, a BrowserFactory contract, or a constants interface.
questions.realTimeExample: A listener class 'implements ITestListener' and overrides onTestFailure() to take a screenshot. TestNG knows only the interface; it calls the method on whatever class the project supplies.

FAIL checkout - button not found

questions.question: Can you create an object of an interface, and how do you call a method of an interface that has not been implemented by any class?
questions.answer: You cannot create an object of an interface directly: new Runnable() without a body does not compile, because an interface has abstract methods with no code to run. What you can do is declare a reference variable of the interface type and assign to it an object of a class that implements the interface. To use an interface that no named class implements, there are three ways. (1) Anonymous class: write new InterfaceName() { ... } with the method bodies inside braces. This creates an object of an unnamed class that implements the interface, on the spot; it looks like instantiating the interface but is not. (2) Lambda expression: if the interface is a functional interface, with exactly one abstract method, a lambda supplies the implementation in one line. (3) Members that already have a body can be called without any implementing class: a static method is called on the interface name, such as Comparator.naturalOrder(), and constants are read as InterfaceName.CONSTANT. A default method does have a body, but it still needs an object, so it is called through some implementation, even an anonymous or lambda one. An abstract method with no implementation anywhere cannot be called, since there is no code to execute.
questions.realTimeExample: Selenium's explicit wait takes a function: wait.until(driver -> driver.getTitle().contains("Home")). The lambda is an implementation of a functional interface created on the spot, with no separate class written.

questions.question: Why can't we write the class logic in the interface instead of the implementing class?
questions.answer: Because an interface and a class have different jobs. An interface defines a contract, what must be done, so that many different classes can each provide their own way of doing it. A class provides the actual behaviour and holds the data. Putting the logic in the interface defeats the purpose: every implementer would share one fixed behaviour, and the flexibility to have different implementations, which is the reason for having the interface, would be lost. There is also a technical reason: an interface cannot hold object state. Its variables are public static final constants, so there are no instance fields, and it has no constructors. Real logic almost always needs data that belongs to each object, such as a driver or a file path, and that can only live in a class. Since Java 8, interfaces can contain default and static methods with bodies, so some logic is allowed. Default methods were added mainly so that new methods could be added to existing interfaces without breaking the classes that already implement them; they are meant for small, general behaviour that depends only on the interface's other methods. If you need shared code together with shared state, the right tool is an abstract class.
questions.realTimeExample: WebDriver declares get(), findElement() and quit() with no logic, because driving Chrome is completely different from driving Firefox. ChromeDriver and FirefoxDriver each supply their own logic, and tests written against WebDriver work with both.

questions.question: How do you achieve multiple inheritance using interfaces? Write a code example.
questions.answer: Java does not allow a class to extend more than one class. The reason is the 'diamond problem': if two parent classes both defined the same method with different code, the child would not know which one to inherit. Interfaces avoid this, because a class may implement any number of them: class C implements A, B. This gives multiple inheritance of type: one object can be treated as any of its interface types. With ordinary abstract methods there is no conflict, since neither interface supplies code; the class writes the single implementation itself. Since Java 8, interfaces can have default methods with bodies, so a conflict can arise when two interfaces declare a default method with the same signature. The compiler then forces the class to override that method and resolve it explicitly. Inside the override, the class can call a specific parent's version using InterfaceName.super.method(). An interface can also extend several other interfaces, and a class can extend one class and implement several interfaces at the same time.
questions.realTimeExample: Selenium's RemoteWebDriver implements WebDriver, JavascriptExecutor and TakesScreenshot together. That is why one driver object can open pages, run JavaScript and take screenshots, and why you cast the driver to the interface for the capability you need.

questions.question: Given two interfaces, one with 4 methods and another with 2, how can you selectively implement only a few methods?
questions.answer: A concrete class must implement every abstract method of the interfaces it implements, so the selection has to be arranged in one of these ways. (1) Adapter class: create an abstract class that implements both interfaces and gives every method an empty or default body. Your real class then extends the adapter and overrides only the methods it needs. This was the classic solution before Java 8. (2) Abstract class: declare your class abstract. It may then implement only some of the methods and leave the rest for its subclasses. (3) Default methods: if you own the interfaces, give the optional methods a default body in the interface itself; implementing classes then override only what they want. This is how TestNG 7 changed ITestListener, so a listener no longer has to write all its methods. (4) Split the interface: if classes often need only part of an interface, the interface is too large. Following the Interface Segregation Principle, break it into smaller interfaces and implement only those required. (5) As a last resort, implement an unwanted method by throwing UnsupportedOperationException, which the Java collections do for read-only lists; it works but shifts the error to run time.
questions.realTimeExample: Before TestNG 7, a listener had to implement all seven ITestListener methods even to use only onTestFailure(), so teams extended TestListenerAdapter instead. Since the methods became default methods, a listener overrides only onTestFailure().

questions.question: Implement the OOP concepts (encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction) for a Savings Bank system.
questions.answer: Design the solution so that each concept has a clear place. Abstraction: an abstract class Account declares what every account can do, deposit, withdraw and calculateInterest, and leaves calculateInterest() abstract because each account type computes it differently. Callers work with Account without knowing the rules inside. Encapsulation: the balance and account number are private. They can be changed only through deposit() and withdraw(), which validate the amount, so the balance can never be set to an invalid value from outside; a getter gives read-only access. Inheritance: SavingsAccount and CurrentAccount extend Account, reusing deposit() and the fields, and adding their own rules such as a minimum balance or an overdraft limit. Polymorphism: run-time polymorphism appears when an Account reference holds a SavingsAccount or a CurrentAccount and the correct calculateInterest() and withdraw() are chosen from the actual object; compile-time polymorphism appears in the overloaded deposit methods. Also mention validation and error handling: reject negative amounts and withdrawals that break the rules by throwing an exception.
questions.realTimeExample: A bank adds a new 'Senior Citizen Savings' account with a higher interest rate. With this design it is one new class extending SavingsAccount that overrides the rate; the existing code that loops over all accounts and credits interest does not change.

questions.question: Write a thread-safe Singleton class. What are its use cases?
questions.answer: A Singleton must create exactly one instance even when several threads call getInstance() at the same moment. The simple lazy version, 'if (instance == null) instance = new ...', is not thread-safe: two threads can both see null and each create an object. Thread-safe options: (1) Eager initialization: create the instance in a static final field. The JVM guarantees that class loading happens once, so it is safe; the cost is that the object is created even if never used. (2) Synchronized method: mark getInstance() synchronized. Safe, but every call takes a lock. (3) Double-checked locking: check for null, synchronize only when it is null, and check again inside the lock. The field must be volatile, otherwise another thread could see a partly constructed object. This is the version interviewers usually ask you to write. (4) Initialization-on-demand holder: a private static inner class holds the instance; it is loaded only when getInstance() is first called, giving lazy and safe creation without locks. (5) Enum singleton: an enum with one value, which is thread-safe and also protected against reflection and serialization tricks. In all class-based versions the constructor is private. Use cases: configuration reader, logger, connection pool, report manager. A WebDriver should not be a plain Singleton in parallel runs; keep one per thread with ThreadLocal.
questions.realTimeExample: ExtentReports must be created once for the whole run, although tests run on eight threads. A Singleton report manager with double-checked locking ensures every thread writes to the same report object instead of creating its own.

questions.question: Explain exception handling in Java.
questions.answer: An exception is an event that interrupts the normal flow of a program at run time, such as dividing by zero, using a null reference or failing to find a file. If it is not handled, the program stops and prints a stack trace. Exception handling lets the program deal with the problem and continue or stop cleanly. Java uses five keywords. try: wraps the code that might fail. catch: follows the try and contains the code that runs when a matching exception occurs; there can be several catch blocks, ordered from the most specific exception to the most general. finally: runs after try and catch whether or not an exception occurred, and is used for cleanup. throw: raises an exception object yourself. throws: placed in a method signature to declare that the method may pass an exception to its caller. Flow: when an exception occurs in the try block, the rest of that block is skipped, the first matching catch runs, then finally, and the program continues after the whole structure. try-with-resources closes resources such as files automatically. Good practice: catch specific exceptions, never leave a catch block empty, include a helpful message, and do not use exceptions for normal control flow.
questions.realTimeExample: A utility reads a test-data file. If the file is missing, the catch block logs 'Test data file not found: users.json' and rethrows a clear exception, and the finally block (or try-with-resources) closes the stream, instead of the run ending with an unexplained stack trace.

questions.question: Explain the complete exception hierarchy. What is the parent class of all exceptions?
questions.answer: The root of the hierarchy is java.lang.Throwable, which itself extends Object. Only Throwable and its subclasses can be thrown and caught. Throwable has two direct subclasses. Error represents serious problems in the JVM or the environment that an application is not expected to recover from, such as OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError and NoClassDefFoundError. Exception represents conditions an application can reasonably handle, and it is the parent class of all exceptions. Exception divides into two groups. Checked exceptions are Exception and its subclasses other than RuntimeException: IOException, FileNotFoundException, SQLException, ClassNotFoundException, InterruptedException. The compiler requires them to be caught or declared. Unchecked exceptions are RuntimeException and its subclasses: NullPointerException, ArithmeticException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, ClassCastException, IllegalArgumentException, NumberFormatException, IllegalStateException. The compiler does not force you to handle them; they usually indicate a programming mistake. So the precise answer is: Throwable is the parent of everything throwable, and Exception is the parent of all exceptions. Selenium's WebDriverException extends RuntimeException, so all Selenium exceptions are unchecked.
questions.realTimeExample: Because NoSuchElementException is unchecked, findElement() can be called without try/catch or a throws clause. Thread.sleep() throws the checked InterruptedException, which is why code using it must catch it or declare 'throws InterruptedException'.

IOException is unchecked? false
ArithmeticException is unchecked? true
buzzWords: Exception Is the Parent of All Exceptions

questions.question: What is the difference between an exception and an error?
questions.answer: Both are subclasses of Throwable and both stop the normal flow, but they differ in cause and in whether the program should try to recover. An Exception is a problem that arises from the application's own code or its inputs: wrong data, a missing file, a null reference, a failed network call. It can be anticipated and handled with try/catch, after which the program can continue. Exceptions are either checked, which the compiler forces you to handle, or unchecked. An Error is a serious problem in the Java Virtual Machine or the system it runs on: running out of memory (OutOfMemoryError), endless recursion (StackOverflowError), or a class that cannot be loaded (NoClassDefFoundError). Errors are all unchecked. An application normally should not catch them, because it usually cannot fix the cause and the JVM may be in an unstable state; the right response is to fix the underlying problem, such as the memory leak or the missing dependency. In short: exceptions are recoverable conditions that the program is expected to handle; errors are critical failures outside the program's control. Note that AssertionError, thrown by test assertions, is technically an Error, which is why 'catch (Exception e)' does not catch a failed TestNG assertion.
questions.realTimeExample: A test catches NoSuchElementException to handle an optional pop-up and carries on: an exception. A suite that keeps every screenshot in memory eventually stops with OutOfMemoryError: an error, fixed by changing the code that holds the memory, not by catching it.

questions.question: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions? Give examples of checked exceptions.
questions.answer: The difference is whether the compiler checks that you handle them. Checked exceptions are verified at compile time. If a method can throw one, the code must either catch it with try/catch or declare it with throws; otherwise it does not compile. They represent problems outside the program's control that a well-written program should expect, mostly involving external resources. They are all subclasses of Exception that are not subclasses of RuntimeException. Examples: IOException, FileNotFoundException, SQLException, ClassNotFoundException, InterruptedException, ParseException, MalformedURLException, CloneNotSupportedException. Unchecked exceptions are not checked by the compiler; handling them is optional. They are RuntimeException and its subclasses and usually result from programming mistakes that should be fixed in the code: NullPointerException, ArithmeticException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, ClassCastException, NumberFormatException, IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException. Errors are also unchecked. Both kinds occur at run time; 'checked' refers only to the compiler's check. When you create a custom exception, extend Exception to make it checked or RuntimeException to make it unchecked.
questions.realTimeExample: new FileInputStream("data.xlsx") does not compile unless FileNotFoundException is handled or declared: checked. driver.findElement(By.id("x")) compiles without any handling and throws NoSuchElementException only if the element is missing: unchecked.

questions.question: What is the difference between throw and throws?
questions.answer: throw is a statement used inside a method body to raise an exception at that moment. It is followed by one exception object, usually created with new: throw new IllegalArgumentException("message"). Execution of the method stops at that line and control goes to the nearest matching catch. Only one exception can be thrown by one throw statement. throws is a clause in the method signature that declares which exceptions the method might pass on to its caller. It is followed by one or more exception class names separated by commas: void read() throws IOException, SQLException. It does not raise anything itself; it warns the caller, who must then catch the exception or declare it in turn. It is required for checked exceptions that the method does not catch, and optional for unchecked ones. In short: throw actually throws an exception, uses an object, appears inside the method and handles one at a time; throws only declares the possibility, uses class names, appears in the signature and can list several. They are often used together: a method declares 'throws' and contains 'throw'.
questions.realTimeExample: A config reader does 'throw new IllegalStateException("Key not found: " + key)' when a property is missing, so the failure message is clear. A test method that calls Thread.sleep() declares 'throws InterruptedException' because it does not handle that checked exception itself.

questions.question: Can we use try without catch? try with finally? Multiple catch blocks with one try? What is the finally block?
questions.answer: A try block cannot stand alone; it must be followed by a catch, a finally, or both. try without catch: allowed when there is a finally block (try-finally), or when it is a try-with-resources statement, which may have neither. In try-finally the exception is not handled; finally runs and the exception then continues to the caller. Multiple catch blocks: allowed. One try can have several catch blocks for different exception types; only the first matching one runs. They must be ordered from the most specific to the most general, because placing a parent type such as Exception first makes the later blocks unreachable and causes a compile error. Since Java 7, one block can catch several unrelated types with the multi-catch form: catch (IOException | SQLException e). The finally block is optional and comes last. It always runs after try and catch, whether an exception was thrown, caught, not caught, or the try returned a value. Its purpose is cleanup: closing files, database connections or the browser. It does not run only if the JVM exits (System.exit) or the process is killed. Avoid putting a return statement in finally, because it overrides the value returned by try and hides exceptions. try-with-resources is the modern replacement for cleanup in finally.
questions.realTimeExample: A database utility opens a connection in try, catches SQLException to log the failing query, and closes the connection in finally (or uses try-with-resources), so connections are not leaked when a query fails halfway through a test run.

questions.question: How do you create and throw a custom exception?
questions.answer: A custom exception is your own exception class, used to report an application-specific problem with a meaningful name instead of a generic exception. Steps: (1) Create a class whose name ends with 'Exception'. (2) Extend Exception to make it a checked exception that callers must handle, or extend RuntimeException to make it unchecked, which is the usual choice in test frameworks because it does not force try/catch everywhere. (3) Add constructors that pass the message to the parent with super(message), and one that also accepts the original cause, super(message, cause), so the root error is not lost when you wrap another exception. (4) Throw it with the throw keyword: throw new InvalidBrowserException("..."). If it is checked, the method must also declare it with throws. (5) Catch it where it can be handled, or let it fail the test with its clear message. Extra fields, such as an error code, can be added when useful. Custom exceptions make failures easier to diagnose and let callers catch one specific situation.

questions.question: How do you handle NullPointerException?
questions.answer: NullPointerException (NPE) is thrown when code uses a reference that points to no object: calling a method on null, reading a field of null, taking the length of a null array, or unboxing a null Integer. The best handling is prevention, not catching. (1) Check before use: if (value != null). (2) Put the constant first when comparing strings: "admin".equals(role) is safe when role is null, whereas role.equals("admin") is not. Objects.equals(a, b) is safe on both sides. (3) Initialize variables and return empty collections instead of null from methods. (4) Use Optional for a value that may be absent: Optional.ofNullable(value).orElse("default"). (5) Use Objects.requireNonNull(value, "message") at the start of a method to fail early with a clear message. (6) Supply defaults: map.getOrDefault(key, "") and System.getProperty(key, "default"). (7) Read the stack trace: it gives the exact line, and since Java 14 the message names the variable that was null. Catching NullPointerException is rarely right, because it hides a defect in the code; fix the cause instead. In Selenium tests the usual causes are a WebDriver that was never initialized, a page object created without the driver, or a missing key in test data.

The driver field was declared in BaseTest but the @BeforeMethod that creates it did not run, because the test was executed by group and the setup method lacked alwaysRun = true. Fixing the setup removed the exception.

questions.question: You hit a ConcurrentModificationException in a test. How do you fix it?
questions.answer: ConcurrentModificationException is thrown when a collection is structurally changed, by adding or removing elements, while it is being iterated, other than through the iterator itself. Despite the name it usually happens in a single thread: a for-each loop over a list that calls list.remove() or list.add() inside the loop. The for-each loop uses an iterator behind the scenes, and the iterator notices that the collection changed underneath it. Fixes, depending on the need: (1) Use the iterator's own remove(): iterate with an explicit Iterator and call iterator.remove(). (2) Use removeIf: list.removeIf(item -> condition), the shortest and clearest form. (3) Collect the items to remove in a second list and call removeAll() after the loop, or build a new filtered list with a stream. (4) Loop backwards with an index, for (int i = list.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--), so removals do not disturb the positions still to be visited. (5) For a map, remove through the entry-set iterator or use map.entrySet().removeIf(...). (6) If several threads really do share the collection, as in parallel tests, use a concurrent collection such as CopyOnWriteArrayList or ConcurrentHashMap, whose iterators do not throw this exception, or better, avoid sharing the collection between threads.
questions.realTimeExample: A test looped over a list of product names and removed the out-of-stock ones inside the for-each loop; it failed on the second iteration. Replacing the loop with products.removeIf(name -> outOfStock.contains(name)) fixed it.

Problem: ConcurrentModificationException
Fix 1 iterator.remove(): [1, 3, 5]
Fix 2 removeIf: [1, 3, 5]
Fix 3 backward loop: [1, 3, 5]
Fix 4 CopyOnWriteArrayList: [1, 3, 5]

questions.question: What is the difference between fail-fast and fail-safe iterators?
questions.answer: The terms describe how an iterator reacts when its collection is modified during iteration. A fail-fast iterator stops immediately by throwing ConcurrentModificationException when it detects that the collection was structurally changed after the iterator was created, except through the iterator's own remove(). It works directly on the original collection and detects changes with an internal counter called modCount, which it compares on each call to next(). The iterators of the ordinary collections in java.util are fail-fast: ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSet, HashMap, TreeMap. The check is made on a best-effort basis and is intended for finding bugs, not for program logic. A fail-safe iterator does not throw the exception. It works on a copy or snapshot of the data, or on a structure designed for concurrent access, so changes made during iteration do not break it. The collections in java.util.concurrent provide them: CopyOnWriteArrayList and CopyOnWriteArraySet iterate over a snapshot taken when the iterator was created, so they do not show later changes; ConcurrentHashMap's iterator is 'weakly consistent' and may or may not show changes made during iteration. The trade-off: fail-safe iterators use more memory or time and may show slightly out-of-date data, in exchange for safety under concurrent modification.

Using a CopyOnWriteArrayList for the shared results list removed the failure.

questions.question: Explain the Java Collections framework and its hierarchy. Which collections have you used in your framework?
questions.answer: The Collections framework is a set of interfaces and classes in java.util for storing and processing groups of objects, with ready-made data structures and algorithms. The hierarchy starts with the Iterable interface, extended by Collection, which has three main child interfaces. List: an ordered collection that allows duplicates and access by index. Implementations: ArrayList, LinkedList, Vector and Stack. Set: a collection of unique elements. Implementations: HashSet (no order), LinkedHashSet (insertion order) and TreeSet (sorted, through SortedSet). Queue: holds elements for processing, usually first-in first-out. Implementations: PriorityQueue, ArrayDeque and LinkedList, with Deque allowing access at both ends. Map is part of the framework but does not extend Collection, because it stores key-value pairs: HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap, Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap. The Collections class provides utility methods such as sort and reverse. In an automation framework: List<WebElement> from findElements() and lists of expected values; Set<String> for window handles and for removing duplicates; Map<String, String> for a row of test data or for configuration; List<Map<String, String>> for a whole sheet of data; and ConcurrentHashMap or ThreadLocal for data shared in parallel runs.

questions.question: What is the difference between Collection and Collections?
questions.answer: The names differ by one letter but they are completely different things. Collection (singular) is an interface in java.util. It is the root interface of the collection hierarchy and represents a group of objects. List, Set and Queue extend it, and it declares the basic operations that all of them share: add(), remove(), contains(), size(), isEmpty(), clear() and iterator(). You use it as a type: Collection<String> names = new ArrayList<>();. Collections (plural) is a utility class in java.util. It cannot be instantiated and contains only static methods that operate on collections: sort(), reverse(), shuffle(), max(), min(), frequency(), binarySearch(), swap(), unmodifiableList(), synchronizedList() and emptyList(). You call its methods through the class name: Collections.sort(list). A parallel pair with the same relationship is Array and Arrays: Arrays is the utility class for arrays. In summary: Collection is an interface that data structures implement; Collections is a helper class with static methods that work on them.

questions.question: What is the difference between List, Set and Map?
questions.answer: They are the three main ways of grouping objects. List: an ordered sequence. Elements keep their insertion order, duplicates are allowed, and each element has an index starting at 0, so get(index) works. Any number of nulls is allowed. Implementations: ArrayList and LinkedList. Use it when order and position matter or duplicates must be kept. Set: a collection of unique elements. Adding a duplicate has no effect and add() returns false. There is no index. HashSet keeps no order and allows one null, LinkedHashSet keeps insertion order, and TreeSet keeps elements sorted. Use it to remove duplicates or for fast 'is it present' checks. Map: stores key-value pairs. It is not a Collection; it is a separate interface. Keys are unique, values may repeat, and a value is looked up by its key. Adding an existing key replaces its value. HashMap has no order, LinkedHashMap keeps insertion order and TreeMap sorts by key. Use it when each item is identified by a key. Uniqueness in a Set and for Map keys is decided by equals() and hashCode().

questions.question: What is the difference between ArrayList and LinkedHashSet?
questions.answer: Both keep elements in insertion order, which is why they are compared, but one is a List and the other a Set. ArrayList implements List. It allows duplicate elements, gives access by index with get(i), and is backed by a resizable array. Checking whether it contains a value means scanning the elements, O(n). LinkedHashSet implements Set. It does not allow duplicates: adding an element that is already present is ignored. It has no index and no get(i) method; you iterate over it. It is backed by a hash table plus a linked list that remembers insertion order, so contains(), add() and remove() are O(1) on average. It uses more memory per element than an ArrayList. Uniqueness is decided by the elements' equals() and hashCode() methods. When to choose: use ArrayList when duplicates are meaningful or you need positions; use LinkedHashSet when you need unique values in their original order, or many 'does it contain' checks. Converting between them is common: new LinkedHashSet<>(list) removes duplicates while keeping the first occurrence of each, and new ArrayList<>(set) gives index access again. Plain HashSet is slightly faster but does not keep any order.
questions.realTimeExample: A test reads the options of a dropdown into an ArrayList. To prove there are no repeated options, it builds a LinkedHashSet from that list and asserts that both have the same size; the set also gives the unique options in display order for the failure message.

questions.question: What is the difference between HashMap and HashSet?
questions.answer: HashMap implements the Map interface and stores key-value pairs. Keys are unique and values can repeat. Data is added with put(key, value) and read with get(key). It allows one null key and many null values. HashSet implements the Set interface and stores single objects, with no duplicates. Data is added with add(element), and there is no get method; you check membership with contains() or iterate. It allows one null element. Internally they are closely related: a HashSet is built on a HashMap. Each element you add to the set is stored as a key in an internal HashMap, with a shared dummy object as the value. That is why a set's elements are unique, just as a map's keys are. Both use hashing, so both depend on correct hashCode() and equals() methods in the stored objects, both give O(1) average time for adding and looking up, neither keeps insertion order, and neither is synchronized. Use a HashMap when each value needs to be found by a key; use a HashSet when you only need a group of unique values.

questions.question: What is the difference between HashMap and Hashtable, and between Hashtable and HashSet?
questions.answer: HashMap versus Hashtable: both store key-value pairs using hashing, but Hashtable is the older class from Java 1.0. (1) Synchronization: Hashtable's methods are synchronized, so it is thread-safe but slower; HashMap is not synchronized and is faster. (2) Nulls: HashMap allows one null key and any number of null values; Hashtable allows neither and throws NullPointerException. (3) Iteration: HashMap uses a fail-fast Iterator; Hashtable also offers the old Enumeration. (4) Status: Hashtable is a legacy class. For thread-safe maps use ConcurrentHashMap, which locks only part of the map and performs much better, or Collections.synchronizedMap(). Hashtable versus HashSet: they differ in kind. Hashtable is a Map of key-value pairs, added with put() and read with get(); it is synchronized and rejects nulls. HashSet is a Set of unique single elements, added with add(); it is not synchronized and allows one null. What they share is hashing, no ordering, and reliance on hashCode() and equals(). In modern code, neither Hashtable nor Vector is used for new work.
questions.realTimeExample: An old framework stored shared test data in a Hashtable so parallel threads could use it. During modernisation it was replaced with ConcurrentHashMap, which gave the same safety with less waiting between threads.

questions.question: What is the difference between HashMap and ConcurrentHashMap, and where would you use each in an automation framework?
questions.answer: HashMap is not thread-safe. If several threads read and write it at the same time without external locking, updates can be lost, the internal structure can be corrupted and iteration can throw ConcurrentModificationException. It allows one null key and null values and is the fastest choice for single-threaded use. ConcurrentHashMap is designed for use by many threads. It does not lock the whole map: reads generally do not lock at all, and a write locks only the bucket being changed, so many threads can work on different parts at once. This makes it much faster than a fully synchronized map such as Hashtable. It does not allow null keys or null values. Its iterators are weakly consistent and never throw ConcurrentModificationException. It also provides atomic operations that combine check and update safely: putIfAbsent(), computeIfAbsent(), compute() and merge(). Note that a sequence of separate calls, such as get() followed by put(), is still not atomic; use those combined methods. In a framework: use HashMap for data owned by one test or one thread, such as a row of test data, values inside a method, or a ThreadLocal map. Use ConcurrentHashMap for anything shared by parallel threads: a cache of loaded configuration or locators, shared counters of results in a listener, or a registry of created test data for cleanup.

questions.question: Which data structure would you use to remove duplicates from a large dataset before validating an API response?
questions.answer: A HashSet, or a LinkedHashSet when the original order must be kept. A Set stores each value only once, and a hash-based set adds and checks elements in constant time on average, so removing duplicates from n records takes O(n) time in a single pass. The alternative of comparing every record with every other, or calling list.contains() inside a loop, takes O(n²) and becomes unusable for large data: a million records would need about a trillion comparisons. Choose the type of set by need: HashSet is the fastest and keeps no order; LinkedHashSet keeps the order in which values first appeared, usually what a test wants; TreeSet returns the values sorted but costs O(log n) per element. For objects such as records with several fields, the class must implement equals() and hashCode() on the fields that define a duplicate, or you can use a Map keyed by the unique field, such as the id, which also lets you keep the latest version of each record. With streams, distinct() does the same using a set internally. To also report which values were duplicated, use the fact that add() returns false for a value already present. For data too large for memory, remove duplicates in the database with DISTINCT or GROUP BY, or process the data in sorted chunks.

questions.question: Which Java 8 to 21 features have you used in automation frameworks?
questions.answer: Java 8, the most used: lambda expressions for short inline functions, such as custom wait conditions; the Stream API for filtering and transforming lists of elements; method references (WebElement::getText); functional interfaces; Optional for values that may be missing; default methods in interfaces, which TestNG listeners rely on; the java.time API (LocalDate, Duration, DateTimeFormatter), used by Selenium 4 waits; and forEach and removeIf on collections. Java 9: List.of(), Set.of() and Map.of() for small immutable test data; private interface methods. Java 10: var for local variables. Java 11: String methods isBlank(), strip(), lines() and repeat(); Files.readString() and writeString(); and the standard HttpClient for API calls without extra libraries. Java 14: switch expressions with arrows that return a value, and more helpful NullPointerException messages. Java 15: text blocks, triple-quoted multi-line strings that make JSON request bodies and SQL readable. Java 16: records, one-line immutable data classes for test data and API models, and pattern matching for instanceof. Java 17 (long-term support): sealed classes. Java 21 (long-term support): virtual threads, record patterns, pattern matching for switch and sequenced collections with getFirst() and getLast(). Mention only the ones you have really used.

questions.question: What are Streams and lambda expressions, and where have they (and better exception handling) improved your framework code?
questions.answer: A lambda expression is a short way to write a function without a name: parameters, an arrow, and a body, such as (a, b) -> a + b. It provides the implementation of a functional interface and replaces verbose anonymous classes. A Stream is a sequence of elements from a source such as a collection, on which you describe operations as a pipeline instead of writing loops. Intermediate operations, such as filter(), map(), sorted(), distinct() and limit(), return a new stream and are lazy; a terminal operation, such as collect(), forEach(), count(), anyMatch() or findFirst(), runs the pipeline and produces the result. A stream does not change its source and can be used only once. In a framework they shorten and clarify code: converting a List<WebElement> to a list of texts; filtering displayed elements; checking that any or all rows meet a condition; finding the first matching element; sorting and comparing lists; and writing custom explicit-wait conditions as lambdas. Exception handling: checked exceptions cannot be thrown from inside a lambda, so wrap them in a helper that converts them to unchecked exceptions; try-with-resources closes files and connections automatically; multi-catch handles several exception types in one block; and Optional replaces null checks for missing values.

questions.question: What does the double colon :: (method reference) mean?
questions.answer: The double colon is the method reference operator, introduced in Java 8. It is a shorter way of writing a lambda expression whose only job is to call one existing method. Instead of text -> text.toUpperCase() you write String::toUpperCase; instead of x -> System.out.println(x) you write System.out::println. The method is not called at that point; a reference to it is passed, to be called later with the arguments supplied by the stream or other caller. Like a lambda, it can be used wherever a functional interface is expected. There are four kinds. (1) Reference to a static method: ClassName::staticMethod, such as Integer::parseInt, equivalent to s -> Integer.parseInt(s). (2) Reference to an instance method of a particular object: object::method, such as System.out::println. (3) Reference to an instance method of an arbitrary object of a type: ClassName::instanceMethod, such as String::toUpperCase or WebElement::getText, where the stream element becomes the object the method is called on. (4) Reference to a constructor: ClassName::new, such as ArrayList::new. Use a method reference when it reads more clearly than the lambda; if extra logic or arguments are needed, a lambda is required.

questions.question: Find duplicate elements in a list using Java Streams.
questions.answer: There are three common stream solutions. (1) With a Set and filter: create a HashSet and keep each element for which set.add(element) returns false. add() returns false when the element is already in the set, so the filter passes only elements seen before. Collect the result into a Set so each duplicate is reported once. This is the shortest solution and takes one pass, O(n). (2) With groupingBy and counting: collect into a map of element to count using Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), Collectors.counting()), then stream over the map entries and keep the keys whose count is greater than 1. This also tells you how many times each value occurs. (3) With Collections.frequency: filter elements whose frequency in the list is greater than 1 and collect to a set. It is easy to read but O(n²), so suitable only for small lists. Function.identity() means 'use the element itself as the key'. Use LinkedHashMap or LinkedHashSet where the order of the results matters.
questions.realTimeExample: A test reads all email addresses from a user table and must report any that appear more than once. The groupingBy approach lists each duplicated address with its count, which goes straight into the defect report.

questions.question: Filter out empty or null strings from a list using Java 8 streams.
questions.answer: Use filter() with a condition that is true for the elements you want to keep, then collect the result. The order of the checks matters: test for null first, because calling a method such as isEmpty() on a null element throws NullPointerException. The && operator stops at the first false condition, so text != null && !text.isEmpty() is safe. To remove strings that contain only spaces as well, trim before checking: !text.trim().isEmpty(), or use !text.isBlank() from Java 11. The checks can also be written as separate steps with method references: filter(Objects::nonNull) followed by filter(text -> !text.isEmpty()). The original list is not changed; a new list is produced. Note that Arrays.asList() accepts null elements while List.of() does not. An alternative without streams, when the list is modifiable, is list.removeIf(text -> text == null || text.isEmpty()).

questions.question: Given an array of car names, capitalize every name longer than 3 characters using streams.
questions.answer: Create a stream from the array with Arrays.stream(array) and use map() to transform each element. Inside map(), apply the condition: if the name has more than 3 characters, convert it, otherwise return it unchanged. A ternary expression does this in one line. Then collect the results with Collectors.toList(), or back into an array with toArray(String[]::new). Clarify what 'capitalize' means, because interviewers use it in two ways: converting the whole word to upper case with toUpperCase(), or making only the first letter a capital with substring(0, 1).toUpperCase() + substring(1). Note the difference between map() and filter(): filter() would remove the short names from the result, while the question asks to keep every name and change only the long ones, which needs map() with a condition. If only the long names are wanted in the output, use filter() first and then map().

questions.question: What is multithreading? Why is it used, and what are its real-world advantages?
questions.answer: A thread is an independent path of execution inside a program. Multithreading means running several threads within one process at the same time; they share the process's memory, such as the heap and static variables, while each has its own stack. On a multi-core processor threads truly run in parallel; on a single core the system switches between them quickly. Why it is used and its advantages: (1) speed, because independent tasks run at the same time instead of one after another; (2) better use of multi-core hardware; (3) responsiveness, because a long task in the background does not freeze the rest of the program; (4) throughput, as a server handles many users at once, one thread per request; (5) lower cost than separate processes, since threads share memory. Real examples: a web server serving thousands of requests, a browser loading several tabs, a download continuing while you keep working, and parallel execution of automated tests. Creating threads: extend Thread, implement Runnable or Callable, or, preferably, use an ExecutorService thread pool. The costs: threads share data, so unsynchronized access causes race conditions and inconsistent results; locks used wrongly cause deadlocks; and bugs are hard to reproduce. Tools for safety are synchronized, volatile, atomic classes, concurrent collections and ThreadLocal.
questions.realTimeExample: A suite of 600 tests that takes five hours on one thread finishes in about 35 minutes with ten threads, each driving its own browser. That is multithreading applied to test execution.

questions.question: How have you handled multithreading in parallel test execution?
questions.answer: In test automation the threads are created by the test runner, so the work is mostly about making the framework safe for them. (1) Thread creation: TestNG starts the threads from testng.xml with parallel='methods', 'classes' or 'tests' and a thread-count; data providers use parallel = true. (2) One browser per thread: the WebDriver is stored in a ThreadLocal<WebDriver>. Each thread calls set() in its setup, get() during the test, and quit() followed by remove() in teardown, so no thread can see another's browser. (3) No shared mutable state: no static WebDriver, wait, page objects or 'current user' variables. Page objects are created inside each test with that thread's driver. (4) Per-thread reporting: the current report entry, such as ExtentTest, is kept in its own ThreadLocal, and the report object itself is thread-safe and created once. (5) Shared data that really must be shared, such as a results counter or a cache, uses ConcurrentHashMap, AtomicInteger or synchronized blocks. (6) Test data: each test uses unique data or takes an account from a thread-safe pool, so threads do not edit the same records. (7) Independent tests, with no order dependency. (8) Resources: per-thread download folders and file names, and a thread count sized to the machine or the Grid.

Replacing it with a ThreadLocal-based DriverManager, and doing the same for the ExtentTest object, made the parallel run reliable.

questions.question: Implement serialization and deserialization in Java.
questions.answer: Serialization converts an object into a stream of bytes so it can be saved to a file, sent over a network or stored in a cache. Deserialization rebuilds the object from those bytes. Java's built-in mechanism works like this. (1) The class implements the java.io.Serializable interface. It is a marker interface with no methods; it only signals that objects of the class may be serialized. Without it, NotSerializableException is thrown. (2) To serialize, wrap an output stream in an ObjectOutputStream and call writeObject(object). (3) To deserialize, wrap an input stream in an ObjectInputStream, call readObject() and cast the result. Details to know: fields marked transient are skipped and come back with default values, which is used for passwords and other sensitive or temporary data; static fields are not serialized, since they belong to the class; every object referred to by a field must also be serializable; and serialVersionUID is a version number for the class, which should be declared explicitly, because if the class changes and the number differs, deserialization fails with InvalidClassException. The constructor is not run when an object is deserialized. In API testing the same words mean converting a Java object (POJO) to JSON and back, done with libraries such as Jackson or Gson, which is the form used most in automation.

questions.question: Write Java code to reverse a string while preserving the position of whitespace.
questions.answer: The spaces must stay at the same indexes while the other characters are reversed around them. Use two pointers on a char array, one starting at the left end and one at the right end. If the left pointer is on a space, move it forward. If the right pointer is on a space, move it backward. When both are on non-space characters, swap them and move both pointers inward. Stop when the pointers meet. Because a space is never swapped, every space keeps its original position, and all the other characters end up in reverse order. This runs in one pass, O(n) time, and uses only the char array. A second method: create a result array of the same length, copy the spaces into their original positions first, then walk the input from the end and place each non-space character into the next free position of the result.

questions.question: Reverse each word of a sentence in place, so that "This is a test." becomes "sihT si a .tset".
questions.answer: Each word is reversed individually while the words stay in their original order. Split the sentence into words on the space character, reverse each word, and join them back with spaces. Reversing a word can be done with new StringBuilder(word).reverse() or with a loop from its last character. Punctuation attached to a word is treated as part of it, which is why 'test.' becomes '.tset'. To keep the exact spacing, including multiple spaces, do not use split; instead walk through the characters, collect each run of non-space characters, and when a space or the end is reached, append the collected word reversed followed by the space. Do not confuse this with reversing the order of the words, where 'This is a test.' would become 'test. a is This'; ask the interviewer which is meant. With streams: Arrays.stream(text.split(" ")).map(w -> new StringBuilder(w).reverse().toString()).collect(Collectors.joining(" ")).

questions.question: Reverse the word order of "Happiest Minds 2026" without changing punctuation.
questions.answer: Here the order of the words is reversed, not the letters inside them, so 'Happiest Minds 2026' becomes '2026 Minds Happiest'. Simple case, no punctuation: split on whitespace, loop from the last word to the first and join with spaces. 'Without changing punctuation' adds a condition: punctuation marks and spaces must stay exactly where they are while only the words change places, so 'Hello, World!' becomes 'World, Hello!'. A split on spaces would move the punctuation along with its word. The reliable method is: (1) find every word, meaning a run of letters or digits, with a regular expression and store them in a list; (2) reverse the list; (3) walk through the original text again and replace the first word with the first of the reversed list, the second with the second, and so on, copying every other character, including commas, spaces and full stops, unchanged. Matcher.appendReplacement does this in one loop.

questions.question: Take "This is a Java Program", remove the spaces, print it, then reverse it. Explain the program.
questions.answer: The task has two steps and the interviewer wants each explained. Step 1, remove the spaces: text.replace(" ", "") replaces every space with nothing and returns a new String, because Strings are immutable; the original variable is unchanged unless the result is stored. replaceAll("\\s+", "") does the same for all whitespace, including tabs. Step 2, reverse: loop from the last index, length() - 1, down to 0 and append each character to a StringBuilder, or use new StringBuilder(text).reverse(). StringBuilder is used instead of adding to a String in a loop, since each String concatenation would create a new object. Both steps can also be done in a single loop: walk the original text from the end and append every character that is not a space. Printing is done with System.out.println. When explaining, mention what each method returns and that charAt(i) reads the character at position i.

An enhanced for loop over toCharArray() could print the characters but does not give the index, so the classic for loop is the right choice here. A follow-up sometimes asked is to print only the characters at even indexes, or the index of each capital letter, both of which are an if condition inside the same loop. questions.question: Write a Java program to check whether a string is a palindrome.
questions.answer: A palindrome reads the same from both ends, such as 'madam' or 'level'. Method 1, two pointers: compare the first character with the last, the second with the second last, and so on, moving inward. If any pair differs, it is not a palindrome; if the pointers meet without a mismatch, it is. This needs at most n/2 comparisons and no extra memory, and it can stop at the first mismatch. Method 2, reverse and compare: build the reversed string, for example with new StringBuilder(text).reverse().toString(), and check text.equals(reversed). It is shorter but creates another string. Decide how to treat case and non-letter characters. For phrases such as 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama', convert to lower case and remove everything except letters and digits before checking. Use equals() for the comparison, never ==. An empty string and a single character are palindromes.
questions.realTimeExample: 'madam' compares m with m, a with a, and stops at the middle d: palindrome. 'selenium' fails at the first comparison, s with m.

level -> true

a -> true

Madam -> false (case-sensitive)

questions.question: Find the first and the last non-repeating character in a string (for example "swiss" gives 'w' as the first).
questions.answer: A non-repeating character occurs exactly once in the string. Step 1: count how often each character occurs, using a LinkedHashMap<Character, Integer> so that the keys stay in the order of first appearance. Step 2: for the first non-repeating character, go through the map in order and return the first key with a count of 1. For the last non-repeating character, keep going and remember the last key with a count of 1, or walk through the string from the end and return the first character whose count is 1. In 'swiss' the counts are s = 3, w = 1 and i = 1, so the first non-repeating character is 'w' and the last is 'i'. This takes two passes, O(n) time. If every character repeats, there is no answer, so return a marker such as null and report that. A solution without a map compares indexOf(ch) with lastIndexOf(ch); the character occurs once when they are equal. It is short but O(n²).
questions.realTimeExample: For 'swiss': 's' occurs three times, 'w' once and 'i' once. Reading left to right, 'w' is the first character that occurs once and 'i' is the last.
questions.expectedOutput:
swiss -> first: w, last: i
automation -> first: u, last: n
aabb -> first: null, last: null
indexOf approach, first: w

questions.question: Write a Java program to remove duplicate characters from a string.
questions.answer: Keep the first occurrence of each character and drop the later ones. Method 1, LinkedHashSet: add every character to a LinkedHashSet<Character>. A set ignores values it already holds, and the linked version keeps the order in which characters were first added. Then build the result from the set. It takes O(n) time. Method 2, without collections: go through the string and append a character to a StringBuilder only when the result does not already contain it, checked with result.indexOf(String.valueOf(ch)) == -1. This is simple but O(n²). Method 3, streams: text.chars().distinct() keeps the first occurrence of each character, which is then collected back into a String. Decide whether the check should be case-sensitive; by default 'A' and 'a' are different characters. This question, removing duplicates, differs from 'find duplicates', which lists the characters that occur more than once, and from 'non-repeated characters', which lists those that occur exactly once.
questions.realTimeExample: 'programming' becomes 'progamin': the second r, the second g and the second m are removed, and the order of the remaining letters is unchanged.
questions.expectedOutput:
LinkedHashSet: progamin
Without collections: progamin
Stream distinct: progamin

questions.question: Write a program to count the occurrence of each character in a string, for example "success" gives s:3, u:1, c:2, e:1.
questions.answer: Use a map in which the key is the character and the value is its count. Loop over the characters; for each one, store its previous count plus one. Three equivalent ways to write the update: map.put(ch, map.getOrDefault(ch, 0) + 1); map.merge(ch, 1, Integer::sum); or check containsKey first. Use a LinkedHashMap to print the characters in the order they first appear, as the expected output shows, or a TreeMap for alphabetical order; a plain HashMap gives no guaranteed order. Then loop over the entries and print key and value. The time is O(n) with a single pass. If only lower-case letters are involved, an int array of size 26 indexed by ch - 'a' does the same job without a map and is a common follow-up. With streams: text.chars().mapToObj(c -> (char) c).collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), LinkedHashMap::new, Collectors.counting())). Decide whether spaces should be counted and whether upper and lower case are the same letter.
questions.realTimeExample: In 'success': s appears at positions 0, 5 and 6, u once, c twice and e once, giving s:3, u:1, c:2, e:1 in order of first appearance.
questions.expectedOutput:
s:3, u:1, c:2, e:1
Alphabetical: c:2 e:1 s:3 u:1

questions.question: Write a Java program to find the most frequent, the least frequent and the second most repeating character in a string.
questions.answer: All three answers come from the same frequency map. Step 1: count each character with a LinkedHashMap<Character, Integer>, ignoring spaces. Step 2: for the most and least frequent, go through the entries once, keeping the entry with the highest count and the entry with the lowest count seen so far. Step 3: for the second most repeating character, keep two values while scanning, the highest count and the second highest count. When a count is higher than the highest, the old highest becomes the second highest; when it lies between the two, it becomes the new second highest. Using a strict comparison means characters tied with the top count are not reported as second. An alternative is to sort the entries by count in descending order and take the second distinct count. State how ties are handled: with a LinkedHashMap and strict comparisons, the character that appears first in the string wins a tie. The whole solution is O(n) for counting plus a pass over the distinct characters.
questions.realTimeExample: In 'mississippi' the counts are m = 1, i = 4, s = 4 and p = 2. The most frequent is 'i' (first to reach 4), the least frequent is 'm', and the second most repeating is 'p' with 2, because 's' ties with the top count.
questions.expectedOutput:
Counts: {m=1, i=4, s=4, p=2}
Most frequent: i (4)
Least frequent: m (1)
Second most repeating: p (2)

questions.question: Count word frequency and print the duplicate words with their counts, for example "cat dog cat" gives cat:2, dog:1.
questions.answer: This is the character-count technique applied to words. Step 1: clean the text if needed, converting to lower case so that 'Java' and 'java' count as the same word, and trimming the ends. Step 2: split into words on whitespace with split("\\s+"), which handles more than one space between words. Step 3: count with a Map<String, Integer>, using merge(word, 1, Integer::sum) or getOrDefault. A LinkedHashMap keeps the words in the order they first appear. Step 4: print all entries for the full frequency, or only the entries whose count is greater than 1 for the duplicate words. Punctuation attached to words, as in 'cat,' and 'cat', would be counted as different words, so remove it first with replaceAll("[^a-zA-Z0-9\\s]", "") when the text is a real sentence. With streams, Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), Collectors.counting()) does the counting.
questions.realTimeExample: For 'java is fun java is cool' the counts are java:2, is:2, fun:1 and cool:1, so the duplicate words are 'java' and 'is'.

questions.question: Remove all vowels from a string, so that "automation" becomes "tmtn".
questions.answer: The shortest way is a regular expression: text.replaceAll("[aeiouAEIOU]", ""). The square brackets form a character class that matches any one of the listed letters, and each match is replaced with an empty string. Adding (?i) at the start of the pattern makes it case-insensitive, so "(?i)[aeiou]" does the same. Without regex, loop over the characters and append to a StringBuilder only those that are not vowels; a quick vowel test is "aeiouAEIOU".indexOf(ch) != -1. Both take O(n) time. The original string is not changed, since Strings are immutable; use the returned value. Variations asked as follow-ups: remove the consonants instead, by reversing the condition or using the negated class [^aeiouAEIOU]; count the vowels removed, by comparing the lengths before and after; or replace each vowel with a symbol such as '*'.
questions.realTimeExample: 'automation' has the vowels a, u, o, a, i, o. Removing them leaves t, m, t, n, which is 'tmtn'; six of the ten letters were vowels.
questions.expectedOutput:
replaceAll: tmtn
Loop: tmtn
Vowels removed: 6
Mixed case: Slnm WbDrvr
Only vowels: auoaio

questions.question: Move vowels to the left, consonants to the middle and special characters to the right of a string.
questions.answer: Classify each character into one of three groups and then join the groups. Create three StringBuilder objects: one for vowels, one for consonants and one for everything else. Loop over the characters once. If the character is a letter, tested with Character.isLetter(ch), check whether it is a vowel using "aeiouAEIOU".indexOf(ch) != -1; append it to the vowel builder if so and to the consonant builder if not. If it is not a letter, append it to the special-character builder. Finally concatenate the three: vowels + consonants + specials. Because characters are appended in the order they are read, each group keeps its original relative order. This is one pass, O(n) time. Clarify with the interviewer where digits and spaces belong; in this solution anything that is not a letter, including digits and spaces, goes to the right-hand group. If digits need their own group, add a fourth builder with Character.isDigit(ch).
questions.realTimeExample: For 'a@bc#de!': the vowels are 'a' and 'e', the consonants are 'b', 'c' and 'd', and the specials are '@', '#' and '!'. The result is 'ae' + 'bcd' + '@#!' = 'aebcd@#!'.
